title: File handling
sub: Worksheet for the 360° experience: File handling
objectives: know how to open a text file, read what is in it and close it again
understand the difference between write mode and append mode
know how to split one line of a file into its separate fields
starter: A program opens scores.txt in write mode, and the file already holds 40 lines of results. Write down what the file holds the moment that line has run, and which mode should have been used to add to it instead.

stations.name: Reading a whole file
stations.fact: A file left open can keep other programs out, and may lose data that was not written yet.
stations.challenge: Why should a program close a file as soon as it has finished with it?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor
head: Program
Marks
Done
rows: A file called notes.txt is already there. Read the whole of notes.txt in one go. Close the file. Display exactly what was in it and nothing of your own.
A file called data.txt is already there, and it may be empty. Read the whole of data.txt. Count every character in it, newlines included. Display characters [the count] and nothing else.

logic.title: Plan the one you found hardest: inputs, what happens to them, what is printed.

stations.name: Reading line by line
stations.fact: A newline is one single invisible character, which is why a stripped line comes out shorter.
stations.challenge: Why is a stripped line one character shorter than the line that was read?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor
head: Program
Marks
Done
rows: A file called words.txt is already there, and it may be empty. Read the first line of words.txt only. Close the file. Strip the newline off that line. Display first [that line]. Then display length [how many characters are left] on the next line.
A file called words.txt is already there, with one word per line, and it may be empty. Read words.txt. Count how many lines it holds. Display lines [that count] and nothing else.

A file called words.txt is already there, with one word per line, and it may be empty. Read words.txt. Display one line for each word, in the form [position] [word], counting the positions from 1. Display none instead, on a line of its own, when the file holds no words.

stations.name: Writing to a file
stations.fact: Write mode creates the file if it is not there, which is handy and dangerous in equal measure.
stations.challenge: What happens to the contents of a file the moment it is opened in w mode?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor
head: Program
Marks
Done
rows: Ask the user for a word. Make a file called out.txt. Write that word into out.txt on one line. Write ready on the next line. Close the file. Then read out.txt back in one go. Display what you read.

Ask the user for a word. Open the file data.txt in write mode, which empties whatever it held. Write that word into data.txt on a line of its own. Close the file. Then read data.txt back. Display [every line in it], one on each line. Then display lines [how many] on the last line.

logic.title: Plan the one you found hardest: inputs, what happens to them, what is printed.

stations.name: Adding to a file
stations.fact: Three modes cover everything you need: r to read, w to write from scratch and a to add on the end.
stations.challenge: Which mode would a visitor log use, and why that one?

rows: Ask the user for a word. Add that word to the end of the file log.txt, on a line of its own. Keep the lines log.txt already holds. Then read the whole of log.txt back. Display [every line in it], one on each line, and nothing else.

Ask the user for a word. Append that word to the file log.txt, on a line of its own. Keep the lines log.txt already holds. Then read the whole of log.txt back. Display latest [the last line]. Then display total [how many lines] on the next line.

stations.name: Records in a file
stations.fact: A file of comma-separated records is a CSV file, and a spreadsheet will open one straight away.
stations.challenge: How does a program find the record for one particular name?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor
head: Program
Marks
Done
rows: A file called data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line, and it may be empty. Read data.txt. Display one line for each record, in the form [word] [number]. Display none instead, on a line of its own, when the file holds no records.

Ask the user for a word to find. The file data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line. Look at every record in data.txt. Display [word] is [its number] when a record matches. Display no record instead when none matches. Then display checked [how many records you looked at] on the next line.

A file called data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line, and it may be empty. Read data.txt. Display no records when it holds none. Otherwise add up every number. Find the word on the record with the highest number. Display total [the numbers added up]. Then display best [that word] on the next line.

stations.name: Putting it together
stations.fact: Skipping blank lines is worth doing every time: a stray newline at the end of a file is very common.
stations.challenge: Plan the two files a sales report program would need.

Ask the user for a limit. The file data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line. Read data.txt. Make a file called picked.txt. Then display picked [how many] on the last line.

keyq: Why does the mode a file is opened in matter more than anything else on that line?
exam: Every line read from a file is measured with len(), and each answer comes out one character bigger than expected. Name the character being counted, and write the line that removes it.
Write a program that adds a new visitor's name onto the end of log.txt without losing the names already in it, and then prints the whole file.
Each line of members.txt holds a name and an age, separated by a comma. Write a program that prints the name of every member aged 16 or over.
